analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal pipeline safety law, adding operator training and cost-benefit analysis for major rules while easing inspection mandates.
analysis.headline: Both House committees signed off in 1995, including a 29-13 Commerce Committee vote, but the bill sat on the House calendar and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the federal rules governing natural gas and hazardous liquid pipelines. It adds real safety requirements — pipeline workers must be trained to spot dangerous operating conditions, and new pipelines must be built to allow internal inspection devices. At the same time, it removes existing requirements: it repeals the mandatory pipeline inspections that had to happen at least every two years, narrows which water crossings must be inspected, drops earthquake and landslide zones from the list of environmentally sensitive areas, and lets rural gas gathering lines escape federal safety rules. It also makes any new safety rule costing more than $25 million a year pass a cost-benefit test and review by industry-heavy technical committees, and lets companies that join a voluntary 'risk management' demonstration get out from under some safety standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Pipeline owners and operators gain the most: fewer mandated inspections, a higher bar for new safety rules, exemptions for rural gathering lines, and the option to substitute company-written risk management plans for federal standards. Communities near drinking-water intakes and people living along pipeline rights-of-way gain from a few new protections, including drinking-water intake areas being flagged as unusually sensitive and penalties for not reporting excavation damage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pipeline operators, with some safety gains for nearby communities

how_it_helps.text: Requires all people who operate and maintain pipeline facilities to be qualified to recognize and react to abnormal operating conditions that may signal danger [S2][S5].
Requires new or replaced gas and hazardous liquid pipeline facilities, where practicable, to be built to accommodate internal inspection devices known as 'smart pigs' [S2][S5].

Requires the Secretary of Transportation, when marking areas unusually sensitive to environmental damage from a hazardous liquid pipeline accident, to consider drinking-water intake locations for community water systems, sole source aquifers, critical wetlands, national parks, and endangered species habitat [S4][S5].
Subjects people who knowingly damage a pipeline while excavating and fail to report it promptly to civil and criminal penalties [S2][S5].
Requires operators of natural gas pipeline facilities to run public education programs, including teaching the public how to use 'one-call' damage-prevention systems before digging [S2][S5].

analysis.who_pays: People who live, work, or draw water near pipelines would bear the added risk from lighter inspection and maintenance requirements: the bill repeals the requirement for facility inspections at least every two years, narrows inspections on navigable waters to those with substantial commercial navigation, and removes earthquake and landslide zones from the unusually-sensitive-areas analysis [S2][S3]. New federal safety standards costing more than $25 million a year would face a cost-benefit certification and industry-weighted committee review before they could take effect, and companies in the voluntary risk-management project could be exempted from some or all otherwise-applicable safety standards [S2][S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near pipelines and drinking-water sources

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the existing requirement that pipeline facilities be inspected at least once every two years and eliminates certain inspection and maintenance requirements for companies transporting gas and hazardous liquids [S2][S5].
It excludes rural gas gathering lines from the definition of 'transporting gas,' removing them from federal safety regulation [S2][S5].
It repeals the requirement to treat earthquake, landslide, and other ground-movement zones as unusually sensitive to environmental damage from a pipeline accident [S2][S5].

It lets the Secretary exempt companies participating in the voluntary risk-management demonstration project from some or all safety standards, and declares those participants in compliance with covered requirements [S2][S5].

Major new safety rules — those costing over $25 million a year — could not be issued unless the Secretary certifies the benefits justify the costs and explains why other options were rejected, a hurdle that could block precautionary rules after a pipeline failure is suspected but not yet quantified [S2][S5].
It repeals the requirement for criminal penalties in one-call notification system regulations and repeals the annual report requirement for the pipeline safety program [S2][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs genuine safety upgrades — operator qualification, smart-pig inspection access, drinking-water protection, excavation damage penalties — with a broad rollback of the existing inspection and reporting regime. The cost-benefit analysis requirement has an honest rationale: it forces the government to show that expensive rules actually reduce risk. But the same structure, combined with repealing the two-year inspection mandate and narrowing water-crossing and ground-movement protections, shifts the burden of proving safety onto the public after the fact rather than requiring inspections up front. Whether the trade was a net win would depend heavily on how aggressively future administrations used the new exemptions.

outcome.mechanism: Both House committees approved it and it was placed on the Union Calendar in June 1995, but no bill to bring it to the House floor ever came, and it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Hearings were held by the Surface Transportation Subcommittee before the bill was introduced, and it was referred to both the Transportation and Infrastructure and Commerce Committees in March 1995 [S7].
The Transportation and Infrastructure Committee reported the bill amended by voice vote on May 1, 1995, as Part I of House Report 104-110 [S7][S3].
The Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported by a recorded vote of 29-13 on May 24, 1995, and reported it amended on June 1, 1995, as Part II of House Report 104-110 [S7][S4].
On June 1, 1995, the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 58 — the House's holding list for bills awaiting floor action [S7][S5].
No further action was ever recorded on the bill, and it never received a vote in either chamber before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S7][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators came out ahead in the narrow sense that the existing biennial inspection requirement, navigable-water inspection rules, and annual reporting stayed on the books unchanged — but the bill's safety upgrades never took effect either, so communities near pipelines kept the pre-1995 rulebook with no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline operators kept the status quo; nobody got the new rules

for.name: Rep. Bud Shuster
for.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with three original cosponsors and steered it through the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which reported it amended by voice vote on May 1, 1995 [S1][S5][S7].

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over pipeline safety standards
for.what_they_did: Considered and amended the bill, ordered it reported by a vote of 29-13 on May 24, 1995, and reported it on June 1, 1995 as Part II of House Report 104-110 [S7][S4].

for.name: Rep. Thomas Petri, Rep. Greg Laughlin, and Rep. Bill Brewster
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill drew five cosponsors total, three Republicans and two Democrats [S1][S6].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought H.R. 1323 to the House floor; after the bill was placed on the Union Calendar on June 1, 1995, no further action of any kind was recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican chairman sponsored it and the five cosponsors split 3 Republicans and 2 Democrats — and the Commerce Committee's 29-13 vote to report it showed broad but not unanimous support; no floor vote occurred, so no party split on passage is recorded [S6][S7].

industries.industry: Natural gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill would repeal the two-year inspection mandate, narrow water-crossing inspections, exempt rural gathering lines, and let participants in the voluntary risk-management project escape some safety standards. It also raises the cost of any major new federal safety rule above $25 million a year and gives industry-weighted technical committees a formal peer-review role over those rules, with the Secretary required to consult national organizations of pipeline owners before appointing some members [S2][S5].

industries.industry: Environmental and drinking-water interests near pipeline corridors
industries.note: The bill would flag drinking-water intakes, aquifers, wetlands, parks, and endangered-species habitat as unusually sensitive to pipeline accidents, but it repeals earthquake and landslide zones from that analysis and narrows which water crossings get mandatory inspection programs [S2][S4].

industries.industry: Pipeline inspection and engineering service providers
industries.note: Repealing the mandatory two-year facility inspections and trimming inspection requirements on navigable waters would reduce demand for mandated pipeline inspection work [S2].
